title: Puerto Rico at night, 2014–2024
placeName: Puerto Rico (main island, Vieques and Culebra)
selectionReason: Chosen by the project author because night-time light in Puerto Rico changed for reasons that are well documented and are not 'development': island-wide blackouts in 2016, 2017, 2020 and 2022, and a long recovery after Hurricane Maria. That makes it a clear test of the observatory's question. Puerto Rico is not connected to any previous project. No people living in or connected to Puerto Rico have been consulted yet; that would be part of any further work.
question: Puerto Rico's night-time light went dark several times in ten years and came back. What does a brighter or darker island mean — and who gets to decide?
summary: Puerto Rico has been selected as the public case study. The place, period, sources and documented events below are real. The chart and grid still show placeholder demo values until the yearly satellite data has been downloaded and processed.

dataset.name: VIIRS Nighttime Lights (VNL) Version 2.2, annual composites — average-masked radiance
dataset.provider: Earth Observation Group, Payne Institute for Public Policy, Colorado School of Mines
dataset.resolution: 15 arc-second grid — roughly 450–500 m across near the equator. One cell can cover several streets, fields, or a whole village.
dataset.unit: nW/cm²/sr (nanowatts per square centimetre per steradian)
dataset.temporalAggregation: One value per year, built from many night-time passes
dataset.processingSummary: The provider builds each annual value from monthly averages of nightly observations, screened for cloud, moonlight, stray light and other effects; the 'masked' layer also removes background and short-lived lights such as fires (Elvidge et al., 2021). For this case study, the values are averaged over a fixed box around Puerto Rico by scripts/prepare_case_study.py.
dataset.license: Described in the Google Earth Engine catalogue as public domain with no restrictions on use or distribution; confirm on the provider's site before publication.

coverage.explanation: Coverage has not been measured yet. Once the data is processed, each year will be labelled from the number of cloud-free observations (the provider's cf_cvg layer).
coverage.validObservationNote: Pending — computed by scripts/prepare_case_study.py from the cf_cvg layer.

comparison.note: Placeholder demo grid — this is not Puerto Rico. It will be replaced by a coarse average of the real data.
comparison.cellSizeLabel: Each square stands in for one ~500 m grid cell

observedChange.statement: Placeholder: real values for Puerto Rico have not been processed yet, so no change is stated here. The chart below shows illustrative demo values only.
observedChange.caveat: Even once real values are shown, they will not establish why light changed or what that change meant for people living there.

limitations: Annual composites can hide short-lived events. An outage lasting weeks or months may barely move a yearly value.
Products are corrected for cloud, moonlight, snow, stray light and other effects; those corrections can differ between years and product versions.
Spatial resolution is coarse: one grid cell (about 450 m across) can mix homes, roads, industry and open land.
Light can come from many sources — streets, vehicles, ports, power plants, backup generators — not only homes.
A change in lighting technology (for example, a switch to LEDs) can change the recorded value without any change in activity.
The selected box includes ocean, which lowers the average radiance; the same box is used every year, so years remain comparable.
NASA cautions that its night-light outage maps should not be used to monitor outages at the level of individual buildings or roads.
Demo content — the chart and grid values are placeholders until the data is processed.
